With $t$ being the time post drug administration and $\tau$ the time post mosquito,
infection, $\alpha(t, \tau)$ and $\beta(t, \tau)$ are respectively the transmission
blocking (TBA) and reducing (TRA) activities as characterized on oocysts. Figures 2a
and 2c show data of $\alpha(t, \tau = 4\,\mbox{dpi})$ and
$\beta(t, \tau = 4\,\mbox{dpi})$ respectively.

The average reduction of parasite load in mosquitoes infected $\tau$ days ago and
biting people treated $t$ days ago can be expressed as

$$
(1 - \alpha(t, \tau))(1 - \beta(t, \tau))
$$

If $h(t)$ is the distribution of times post drug administration in the population of
treated humans, the average reduction $q(\tau)$ of parasite load in mosquitoes infected
$\tau$ days ago due to 1 bite on treated people then reads

$$
q(\tau) = \int_0^{+\infty}(1 - \alpha(t, \tau))(1 - \beta(t, \tau))h(t)dt
$$

Among mosquitoes infected $\tau$ days ago, if $\lambda(\tau)$ is the ratio of the
parasite average load expressed relative to what we would get in total absence of
treatment in the human population then

$$
\frac{d\lambda}{d\tau} = -(1 - q(\tau)) a p \lambda(\tau)
$$

with

$$
\lambda(0) = 1
$$

leading to 

$$
\lambda(\tau) = \exp\left[-ap\int_0^\tau(1 - q(u))du\right]
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of humans who received treatment and $a$ is the mosquito
biting rate. If $f$ is the relationship between the parasite load and the mosquito
infectiousness, then the reduction of infectiousness due to TBA and TRA reads:

$$
\int_0^{+\infty}e^{-g\tau}f(\lambda(\tau))d\tau
$$

where $g$ is the mosquito death rate.
